facts.claim: The title track "Celebrants" opens Nickel Creek's fifth studio album, Celebrants, which came out March 24, 2023 on Repair Records / Thirty Tigers.

The album was produced, recorded and mixed by Eric Valentine, who also produced Nickel Creek's A Dotted Line. Bassist and producer Mike Elizondo also took part, playing bass and acting as another set of ears.
The trio are Sara Watkins on fiddle, Sean Watkins on guitar and Chris Thile on mandolin. Elizondo joined them on bass.
The album was recorded in Nashville's RCA Studio A in 2021, with Eric Valentine producing and Mike Elizondo on bass.

Sean Watkins said the band got about four weeks in the studio. Producer Eric Valentine is friends with Dave Cobb, who generously let them use the room. Valentine put microphones everywhere, some 30 to 40 feet behind the band.
The album was shaped by the pandemic shutdown. Sean Watkins estimated 75 or 80 days of collective writing before the month of recording.
The album's origin was a 2020 interview marking the 20th anniversary of the band's debut album. It made the trio nostalgic and sparked the new record.
NPR describes the title track's image of heaven in a cathedral rebuilt nightly together as celebrating the simple act of choosing to come together in community.
The band wrote the album the way one might write a novel, so each track contextualizes the ones before and after it. Sara Watkins said they wanted the songs to relate to each other.

Celebrants was Nickel Creek's first release since 2014's A Dotted Line. The trio spent the gap on solo careers and other projects. Their debut was produced by Alison Krauss, and This Side (2002) won a Grammy.

research.lineage: Nickel Creek sits in progressive acoustic bluegrass and Americana, the tradition the trio made their name in before expanding it with theatrical, suite-like arrangements.

draft:
"My God, it's good to see you" is how **Celebrants** begins, and it sounds less like a lyric than the first thing out of someone's mouth at the door. Nickel Creek put that greeting at the very top of their fifth album. It was their first record since 2014's *A Dotted Line*, shaped by the pandemic shutdown and by something like 75 or 80 days of writing together before a month in the studio. The song is a reunion. What makes it sting is that it's also an apology.

The chorus raises a glass, "Sing ho for the gatherings," and then admits we "took 'em for granted then." The relief and the shame arrive in the same breath and never settle each other. The second verse goes further and turns into a real confession: "That was me preaching communion / Even as I prayed for space." The narrator wanted solitude, got more of it than anyone asked for, and now has "about lost my taste for it." That's a hard thing to say out loud at a party. The song doesn't tidy it into a lesson. Even the homecoming takes effort, with "a couple cocktails / Just to pick up the threads," the slightly awkward drinks it takes for old friends to find each other again.

The band plays it like the feeling it describes. Acoustic guitar strums at a relaxed, steady clip over a walking bass line, a snare holds the backbeat, and the mandolin runs melodic lines through the middle. A fiddle lays long, sustained notes underneath. The lead voice is clear and conversational, and then the other voices fold in with a higher harmony until it's a blended crowd. That's the lyric's point made in sound: one person talking, then a room singing. Eric Valentine recorded the album at RCA Studio A in Nashville, and Sean Watkins said Valentine placed microphones everywhere, some 30 to 40 feet behind the band. You can hear the room breathe around them.

This is progressive acoustic bluegrass, the string-band language the trio built their name on, with a drum backbeat pushing it toward Americana. The real move is in the closing image. Heaven has "always been in this cathedral / That we all / Rebuild nightly together." It isn't a church you inherit. It's one you have to put back up every time you show up for each other.

It sticks because it lets you feel two things at once: the joy of walking back into a room full of people you love, and the quiet guilt of knowing you didn't love it enough the first time.
